(CNN)  -- Clashes between Somalia's transitional government and the Al-Shabab militia left 103 people dead and 420 others wounded, Somali officials said Friday. The fighting in Mogadishu between the rebel group and the government has raged for nine days. The fighting in Mogadishu between the rebel group and the government has raged for nine days, said Farhan Ali Mohamud, information minister of the Somali government. Human rights groups deplored the high number of casualties, urging both sides to comply with international law in respect to the civilian population. Thousands of families have fled the capital, Mogadishu, seeking a safer environment in camps south of the city. "The people of Somalia have once again been subjected to unbearable violence," said Pascal Mauchle, head of the International Committee of the Red Cross in Somalia. "The daily struggle for survival is exhausting their capacity to cope." Humanitarian groups expressed concern, too, that Somalis will not have access to medical care. The international medical agency Doctors Without Borders said it was forced to close an outpatient clinic in Mogadishu to ensure safety for its staff. "With so few medical facilities available in Somalia, it is crucial that people are able to access those that are still functioning," said Alfonso Laguna, head of the agency in the region. The new round of fighting stems from an interpretation of sharia law, or Islamic law, the spokesman said. Somalia's new President Sheikh Sharif Ahmed has recently approved implementing sharia law, but the rebel group wants the country to institute a stricter form. A spokesman for the rebel group said it has recruited many fighters for the battle against the government. "It is not only Somali jihadists that are fighting in Mogadishu against the government. There are also foreign Muslim jihadist brothers who are fighting side by side with us," said Sheikh Hassan Ya'qub, a spokesman for al-Shabaab. Abdiraman Abdi Shakur Warsame, minister of international cooperation for Somalia's transitional government, issued a stern warning to the rebels in an address to a young audience celebrating Somali youth day at the capital. "The government is determined to defend itself from these religious gangs who are covering in the name of Islam and I assure you that in the course of coming days, we will eliminate these elements and some of them will be forced out of the country," Warsame said. The U.S. Embassy in Kenya released a statement about the fighting. "The extremists who are instigating these attacks have no regard for the well-being of Somalis and are undermining the peaceful efforts of the legitimate government to further national reconciliation," the statement said. "The United States is particularly disturbed at reports that foreign fighters and those who rejected dialogue in 2006 are participating in this effort to forcibly remove a legitimate Somali government from power." Journalist Mohamed Amiin Adow contributed to this report.

# Escalating Violence in Mogadishu: A Humanitarian Crisis Deepens

Somalia's capital has once again become the epicenter of devastating conflict, as fierce clashes between the country's transitional government forces and Al-Shabab militants have left a trail of destruction across Mogadishu. Over the course of nine consecutive days of fighting, the violence has claimed the lives of 103 people, while an additional 420 individuals have sustained injuries, according to reports emerging from the besieged city. The intensity and duration of this latest round of fighting underscore the fragility of Somalia's security situation and the devastating toll it continues to exact on ordinary civilians caught in the crossfire.

## International Condemnation and Calls for Restraint

The staggering casualty figures have prompted swift condemnation from human rights organizations and humanitarian groups operating both within Somalia and internationally. These organizations have expressed deep alarm over the scale of civilian harm resulting from the conflict, emphasizing that both the transitional government and Al-Shabab forces bear responsibility for protecting non-combatants caught in the crossfire. In their statements, these groups have issued urgent appeals to all parties involved in the fighting, demanding strict adherence to international humanitarian law, which mandates the protection of civilian populations during armed conflict. The persistent violation of these principles, they argue, has transformed Mogadishu into one of the most dangerous urban battlegrounds in the world for ordinary residents simply trying to survive.

## Mass Displacement and the Struggle for Safety

The human cost of this renewed violence extends far beyond the immediate casualties, as thousands of families have been forced to abandon their homes in search of safety elsewhere. Fleeing the chaos and destruction engulfing Mogadishu, displaced residents have made their way to makeshift camps situated south of the city, hoping to find refuge from the fighting that has made daily life in the capital untenable. These displacement camps, however, often lack adequate infrastructure and resources to support the growing number of people seeking shelter within them. Compounding this crisis is the severe shortage of accessible medical care, leaving injured and vulnerable populations with few options for treatment as the conflict continues to rage.

## Medical Services Collapse Under Pressure

The already precarious state of healthcare access in Mogadishu suffered a further blow when Doctors Without Borders (Médecins Sans Frontières), one of the few organizations still providing critical medical services in the war-torn city, announced the closure of one of its outpatient clinics. The organization cited escalating safety concerns as the primary reason for this difficult decision, highlighting the increasingly perilous environment in which humanitarian workers must operate. This closure represents a significant setback for Somalis who already face immense obstacles in accessing basic healthcare, further straining the limited medical infrastructure that remains operational amid the ongoing violence.

## Roots of the Conflict: A Battle Over Religious Interpretation

At the heart of this latest surge in violence lies a fundamental disagreement over the implementation of sharia law within Somalia. Al-Shabab, the militant Islamist group at the center of the conflict, has been pushing for a considerably stricter interpretation and application of Islamic law than what has been sanctioned by President Sheikh Sharif Ahmed's transitional government. This ideological rift has fueled the group's determination to challenge governmental authority through armed confrontation. Reports indicate that Al-Shabab has bolstered its ranks by recruiting both domestic Somali fighters and foreign combatants, suggesting an internationalization of the conflict that could have broader implications for regional stability and the future trajectory of the fighting in Mogadishu and beyond.

# Crisis Deepens in Mogadishu as Fighting Enters Ninth Day

Mogadishu has been engulfed in nine consecutive days of fierce urban warfare between Somalia's transitional federal government forces and the Al-Shabab militia, a conflict rooted in deep disagreements over the interpretation and strictness of sharia law implementation across the country. What began as ideological disputes over religious governance has escalated into one of the most devastating rounds of violence the capital has witnessed in recent memory, plunging the city into a severe humanitarian emergency.

The human toll of the fighting has been staggering. According to reports compiled by monitoring groups, the clashes have claimed the lives of 103 people, while an additional 420 individuals have sustained injuries ranging from moderate to critical. These casualty figures reflect not only combatants but also a significant number of civilians caught in the crossfire, as fighting has often taken place in densely populated residential neighborhoods where government forces and Al-Shabab militants engage in street-by-street combat.

The violence has triggered a mass exodus from the capital, with thousands of terrified residents abandoning their homes and neighborhoods in search of safety. Families have been forced to flee with little more than what they could carry, joining the ranks of Somalia's already substantial internally displaced population. Many have sought refuge in makeshift camps on the outskirts of Mogadishu or in neighboring regions, further straining already limited resources and humanitarian infrastructure.

International human rights organizations have been vocal in expressing alarm over the deteriorating situation. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) has highlighted the increasingly precarious conditions facing civilians trapped in conflict zones, emphasizing the urgent need for all parties to respect humanitarian principles and allow safe passage for those seeking to escape the violence. Doctors Without Borders (Médecins Sans Frontières), which operates critical medical facilities in the region, has raised serious concerns about the strained capacity of healthcare infrastructure to cope with the influx of wounded patients, noting that medical staff are operating under extremely difficult and dangerous conditions.

Adding a troubling new dimension to the conflict is the reported involvement of foreign jihadist fighters who have joined Al-Shabab's ranks alongside local Somali rebels. This influx of international militants has raised concerns among regional and international observers about the growing transnational nature of the insurgency and its potential to further destabilize not just Somalia, but the broader Horn of Africa region.

As the fighting shows no immediate signs of abating, aid organizations continue to call for humanitarian corridors and increased access to deliver critical medical supplies and assistance to those affected. The international community faces mounting pressure to address both the immediate humanitarian needs of displaced civilians and the underlying political and ideological tensions fueling this protracted and increasingly deadly conflict.

Somalia has experienced prolonged periods of conflict since the collapse of its central government in 1991. The nation has struggled with the presence of militant groups, particularly al-Shabaab, which has conducted numerous attacks against government forces, African Union peacekeepers, and civilian targets. The international community, including the African Union Mission in Somalia (AMISOM) and its successor missions, along with various UN agencies, has been involved in efforts to stabilize the country. # Fighting Escalates in Mogadishu as Somali Forces Clash with Al-Shabab

**MOGADISHU, Somalia** — Intense fighting erupted across multiple districts of Somalia's capital this week as government forces backed by African Union troops engaged in fierce clashes with Al-Shabab militants, marking one of the most significant escalations of violence in the city in recent months.

According to Somali security officials, the fighting began after Al-Shabab launched a coordinated assault targeting government checkpoints and a police training facility on the outskirts of Mogadishw, prompting a swift military response. The clashes quickly spread to at least three neighborhoods, with mortar fire and small arms exchanges reported well into the night.

## Casualty Figures Remain Fluid

Somali Ministry of Information officials say at least 23 people have been killed since fighting began, including 14 suspected militants, six government soldiers, and three civilians caught in the crossfire. Local hospitals report treating more than 40 wounded, though officials caution that these figures are preliminary and likely to rise as communication with affected areas remains difficult.

"The situation on the ground is still evolving," said a spokesperson for the Somali National Army. "Our forces have regained control of several key positions, but pockets of resistance remain."

Al-Shabab, in a statement circulated through its usual media channels, claimed responsibility for the initial attack and asserted that its fighters had inflicted heavy casualties on government forces — claims that could not be independently verified.

Residents in affected neighborhoods described scenes of panic as families fled their homes amid the fighting. "We heard explosions all night. My children haven't stopped crying," one Mogadishu resident told local reporters, speaking on condition of anonymity for fear of reprisal.

## Regional and International Reactions

The African Union Transition Mission in Somalia (ATMIS), which maintains a peacekeeping presence in the country, confirmed that its forces provided support to Somali troops during the clashes. In a statement, ATMIS reaffirmed its commitment to "supporting the Federal Government of Somalia in its efforts to degrade Al-Shabab's operational capacity."

The United States, which has conducted periodic airstrikes against Al-Shabab targets in coordination with Somali authorities, condemned the attack. A State Department spokesperson called on "all parties to protect civilian lives" and reiterated Washington's support for Somalia's counterterrorism efforts.

The United Nations Assistance Mission in Somalia (UNSOM) expressed concern over the rising civilian toll, urging both government forces and militants to exercise restraint in populated areas. "Every effort must be made to protect civilians caught in this conflict," a UN spokesperson said.

Neighboring Kenya and Ethiopia, both of which have troops contributing to regional stabilization efforts, also issued statements of solidarity with the Somali government, with Kenyan officials reiterating concerns about cross-border security implications.

## A Persistent Threat

Al-Shabab, which has waged an insurgency against the Somali government for more than 15 years, continues to control swathes of rural territory despite sustained military campaigns by Somali forces and international partners. The group has been increasingly pushed out of major urban centers in recent years but retains the capacity to launch high-profile attacks in Mogadishu and beyond.

Analysts say this week's clashes underscore the fragile security situation in the capital despite recent gains touted by the Somali government.

"Al-Shabab remains a resilient and adaptive threat," said one regional security analyst. "Even as territorial control shrinks, their ability to strike at the heart of government power in Mogadishu remains a serious concern."

Somali officials say military operations to clear remaining militant positions are ongoing, and additional security measures have been implemented across the capital, including increased checkpoints and a nighttime curfew in some districts.

The Somali government has not yet announced a formal death toll update, and CNN could not independently confirm claims made by either side regarding the scale of casualties. This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.

*CNN's team continues to monitor the situation in Mogadishu. Contributions to this report came from local sources in Somalia.*

# Nine Days of Fighting Rock Mogadishu, Leaving Scores Dead and Thousands Displaced

**MOGADISHU** — For a ninth consecutive day, heavy fighting has convulsed the Somali capital, as insurgent forces clashed with government troops and African Union peacekeepers in a battle that has left residential neighborhoods in ruins and sent waves of civilians fleeing the city.

## Death Toll Continues to Climb

Local hospitals and medical committees report that the death toll from the fighting has risen sharply, with officials citing figures ranging into the hundreds since the violence erupted. Mortuary workers and volunteer ambulance crews describe overwhelmed facilities, with the wounded — many of them women and children caught in mortar and artillery crossfire — arriving faster than medical staff can treat them.

"We have never seen fighting this intense for this long," said one hospital administrator, speaking on condition of anonymity due to security concerns. "The wards are full, the hallways are full. We are running out of space and supplies."

Casualty figures remain difficult to verify independently, as journalists face significant risks moving through active combat zones, and rival factions have offered conflicting death toll estimates.

## Mass Displacement Strains Already Fragile City

The human toll extends far beyond the casualty figures. Aid organizations estimate that tens of thousands of residents have fled their homes over the past nine days, joining the ranks of Somalia's already massive displaced population.

Families are reportedly streaming out of the hardest-hit districts on foot, carrying whatever belongings they can manage, seeking shelter in makeshift camps on the city's outskirts or in neighboring regions. Humanitarian workers warn that the sudden influx is straining limited resources, with shortages of clean water, food, and basic medical care becoming acute in areas absorbing the displaced.

"Every time there is a surge in fighting, we see this same pattern — families running with nothing, ending up in camps that are already stretched beyond capacity," said one aid coordinator working in the region.

## U.S. Embassy Points to Foreign Fighters

Amid the escalating violence, the U.S. Embassy in Nairobi, Kenya, which handles diplomatic affairs related to Somalia, issued a statement addressing the role of foreign combatants in the conflict. Embassy officials expressed concern over what they described as the growing presence of foreign fighters aligned with insurgent groups operating in Mogadishu.

An embassy spokesperson said the United States remains "deeply concerned" about reports that fighters from outside Somalia have joined the insurgency, characterizing their involvement as part of a broader effort by extremist elements to destabilize the country and undermine the Transitional Federal Government.

The statement did not provide specific numbers of foreign combatants believed to be involved but reiterated Washington's support for African Union peacekeeping forces and the internationally backed transitional government.

## Uncertain Path Forward

As the fighting shows little sign of abating, residents describe a city on edge, with markets shuttered, streets emptied of ordinary commerce, and the constant threat of stray fire or shelling looming over daily life.

Diplomatic and humanitarian officials continue to call for a ceasefire, though efforts to broker even a temporary halt to the violence have so far produced no breakthrough. With displacement camps swelling and hospitals stretched thin, aid groups warn that the humanitarian consequences of the prolonged clashes will likely be felt long after the guns eventually fall silent.

*This is a developing story.*

# Somalia's Enduring Crisis: Civilians Caught Between Government Forces and Al-Shabab

*A Look at the Human Cost of a Conflict Now Entering Its Second Decade*

MOGADISHU — The queue outside Banadir Hospital forms before dawn. Mothers carry children with shrapnel wounds; elderly men wait for treatment of injuries sustained not in active combat, but in the slow grinding aftermath of explosions that have become routine in Somalia's capital.

This is the texture of a conflict that rarely makes sustained international headlines but continues to reshape—and end—lives across the Horn of Africa.

## A Conflict Rooted in Governance and Religious Authority

The war's origins trace to competing visions of governance following the collapse of Siad Barre's government in 1991. Al-Shabab, which emerged from the Islamic Courts Union in the mid-2000s, has framed its insurgency as a defense of strict sharia interpretation against what it calls an illegitimate, foreign-backed government.

"We are implementing the law of Allah, not the law of Western occupiers," said a spokesperson identifying himself as part of Al-Shabab's media wing in a statement circulated to journalists. "The Mogadishu administration enforces secular corruption dressed in the language of Islam."

Somali government officials reject this characterization entirely.

"Al-Shabab does not represent Islamic law—they represent a distortion used to justify terrorism against fellow Muslims," said a Somali Ministry of Information official. "Our constitution recognizes sharia as a source of law, interpreted through legitimate institutions, not imposed through massacre."

This dispute over religious and legal legitimacy remains central to the conflict's持续ance, with both sides invoking Islamic jurisprudence to justify fundamentally different projects: one an internationally recognized federal government, the other an insurgency controlling significant rural territory.

## Counting the Cost

Precise casualty figures remain contested and difficult to verify independently, complicated by the remoteness of conflict zones and restricted journalist access. However, aggregated data from monitoring organizations, UN agencies, and academic conflict trackers suggest:

- Tens of thousands of civilians have been killed since the insurgency intensified after 2006, with some estimates suggesting cumulative deaths from the broader conflict since 1991 exceeding 500,000.
- The UN has documented thousands of civilian casualties in recent years alone, with explosive devices and targeted attacks on markets, hotels, and government buildings among the leading causes.
- Somalia consistently ranks among the world's largest sources of internally displaced persons, with over 3 million people displaced internally as of recent assessments—many multiple times over, fleeing successive waves of violence, drought, and famine.

"Every displacement camp represents a story of survival, but also profound loss," said a UN OCHA field officer speaking on background. "Families arrive with almost nothing. Many have lost members to violence, to disease along the journey, or to the drought conditions that compound this crisis."

## Life Under Contested Authority

In areas under Al-Shabab control, residents describe a parallel justice system—one that supporters within the movement portray as swift and incorruptible.

"There is no bribery here. There is no delay in justice," the Al-Shabab spokesperson claimed, referencing the group's court system, which has drawn both grudging respect for reducing certain forms of petty crime and international condemnation for punishments including amputations and executions carried out publicly.

Human rights organizations have extensively documented harsh punishments under this system, alongside the conscription of child soldiers and restrictions on movement, education for girls, and access to humanitarian aid in contested areas.

Government-controlled areas face their own governance challenges. Corruption remains endemic, security force abuses have been documented by rights monitors, and basic services often fail to reach populations even in areas nominally under federal or state control.

"We are fighting for a Somalia where courts function through due process, not fear," the government spokesperson said. "That does not mean we have achieved this yet everywhere. But the alternative is submission to men who claim divine authority while burying children in unmarked graves."

## The Humanitarian Machinery Under Strain

Aid organizations operate under extraordinarily difficult conditions. Access negotiations with Al-Shabab—required to reach populations in insurgent-held territory—are fraught and sometimes fail entirely, leaving vulnerable populations cut off from food assistance during climate-driven famine conditions that have compounded the conflict's toll.

"We are not just fighting bullets and explosives," said one humanitarian coordinator with an international NGO operating in south-central Somalia. "We're fighting logistics nightmares, access denials, and a climate crisis that has turned drought into a weapon nobody intended but everybody suffers from."

Famine conditions in 2011 and again in 2022 killed tens of thousands, with children under five disproportionately represented among the dead—a toll directly connected to conflict dynamics that restricted humanitarian access and disrupted agricultural livelihoods.

## No Clear Resolution in Sight

African Union forces, transitioning toward a new AU mission structure, continue operating alongside Somali National Army units in an uneasy security arrangement. Al-Shabab, despite periodic government offensives claiming territorial gains, retains capacity for high-profile attacks in Mogadishu and beyond.

For civilians, the war's ideological and legal disputes remain secondary to daily survival calculations: which roads are safe, which checkpoints to avoid, whether aid convoys will arrive before the next displacement.

"Politicians and fighters talk about sharia, about sovereignty, about legitimacy," said a Mogadishu shopkeeper who declined to give his name, citing safety concerns. "We talk about whether the market will be bombed today."
